Technology can fail, so we have to be ready to respond. Even a grease fire in a kitchen. That sums up the message in this short from the 1970s. Oh, and we learn to turn off "Tattletales" (a Mark Goodson-Bill Todman Production) during a brown out. The score is pretty good. Creepy electronic music at the start and a Hammond organ at the end. Peter Thomas, who voiced all kinds of commercials for big companies, and documentaries, appears on camera in addition to narrating. The farmhouse flashback has a curious cat in the kitchen.

So this film purports, in it's all too roundabout way, that man hasn't learned anything from technology. The more things change, the more they stay the same. Interesting topic, though it does take it's sweet time to explain it, then at the end you're like, that's it? Meh.

On second thought, the film isn't that bad, even if it is dated. The moral, that everyone should know how to respond to a "technological failure", is sound and some useful example are given. Overall though, the film seems to meander, as another reviewer put it, and the "pioneer days" comparison is questionable on several levels. Even then people were depended on technology that was beyond them. The kerosene shown being poured into lamps was refined in a process no farmer was likely to know or be able to replicate.

After reading dynayellow's review, I watched this film again thinking I missed something. I did: it rips off the far superior first episode of James Burke's original "Connections" series. rv: the film starts with an old steamboat going down river leading one to think that this film is going to be pretty dry. for god's sake, keep watching! the film gets nuttier as it goes along and every scene with JB, the tobacco tycoon is pure gold. who knew boss hogg went to the strasberg school? the guy's pretty hard core about getting people to smoke his brand of cigarettes. even taking out ads in high school papers. this is a must watch if depictions of southern good 'ol boys tickle your fancy and of course if you like dream sequences of baseball players using a giant cigarette as a bat.…

Though this production is roughly twice as long as many of the films featured in the archives, don't be reluctant to have a look. There's some corny actors and reams of goofy dialogue, but the film is successful in illustrating tobacco companies' efforts to establish brand loyalty and get, as JB, the bald-headed boss in the film proclaims, "every man, woman and child in the country" smoking heavily. Up in Smoke does show its age, but its concerns are still relevant. One of the best films I've discovered in the archives. I like the music that accompanies the scientist who is constantly trying…

This is kind of a screwballcomedy about tobacco industry. But but... gags are no good and - of course - only un-intentional stuff is funny. Some good scenes here and there but genarally this film is just poor acting, poor dialogue etc. Up In Smoke is way too long and gets boring in middle, but the last scene is so good that it makes the whole film worth watching. Nicely tinted colour too. ***/*****
